warmup.q: A JVM in a container started with --pids-limit 64 creates platform threads in a loop, each one waiting on a latch. About how many does it get before OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread?
options: As many as the heap has room for
Thousands: the pids limit counts processes, not threads
warmup.why: The pids limit counts tasks, and every thread is a task. The JVM's own threads (GC, JIT compilers, carriers and the rest) take a good part of the 64 before your code starts any, so in the lab box it stopped at 42 one run and 50 another. The heap has nothing to do with it.

sections.h: Threads exist so one program can wait on many things at once
sections.html:
A payment service gets 50 authorization requests in the same second, and each one waits 120 ms for the card issuer. With a single line of execution, request 2 starts only after request 1 has its answer. 50 requests take 6 seconds, and the CPU sits idle for almost all of it. You want all 50 in flight at once, each waiting on its own.

The first way is the one lesson 2 of this track built: one process per request. fork a copy for each request and the kernel runs the copies side by side. Old web servers worked like that. It's a poor fit for a JVM service. Processes don't share memory, so every copy has its own heap, its own cache of exchange rates and its own connection pool, and the 20 Oracle connections you budgeted become 20 per copy.

What you want is several lines of execution inside one process, all sharing its memory. Each line needs only three things of its own: a place in the code (the program counter from lesson 1), its own registers, and its own stack, the region of memory that holds each method call's local variables and the address to return to. One such line is a thread.

Linux builds threads and processes from the same part. The kernel schedules one kind of thing (it picks which one runs on each CPU, and for how long), a task: a program counter, registers, a stack and an ID, the TID. When clone creates a task, flags say what the new task shares with its creator. These are the flags on every clone the JVM made in lesson 1:

CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|...

fork passes none of the sharing flags, so its new task gets copies of everything and becomes a new process. A thread is a task created with flags that say "share, don't copy". CLONE_VM shares the memory, CLONE_FILES the open files, CLONE_SIGHAND the signal handlers, and CLONE_THREAD puts the new task in the caller's thread group. A process, as you know it, is a thread group: a set of tasks that share one memory.

That explains a field you met in lesson 2. A process's PID is the TID of its first task, and the Tgid (thread group ID) line in /proc/<pid>/status shows that same number in every thread of the group. A signal sent with kill <pid> goes to the group as a whole.

The figure below is the model for the rest of this lesson. A process is a box of shared memory with tasks in it. The JVM decides how Java threads map onto those tasks, and the later sections look at the two ways it does that.

sections.h: A JVM is a few dozen tasks before your code starts any
sections.html:
Each task in a process shows up as a directory under /proc/<pid>/task/, named after its TID, with its own status, stat and comm (the thread's name) files. The JVM names its threads, so you can take a census by name. Here are the top lines for a small demo service in the lab box:

     13 ForkJoinPool-1-
      2 java
      2 C2 CompilerThre
      1 VM Thread
      1 VM Periodic Tas

That service has 36 tasks, though it starts only three ordinary threads of its own (plus 1,000 virtual threads, the subject of the last section). The kernel keeps only the first 15 characters of a thread's name, so ForkJoinPool-1-worker-11 becomes ForkJoinPool-1-. Most of the rest belong to the JVM: garbage collector threads (GC Thread#0, G1 Conc#0), the JIT compilers (C2 CompilerThread0, C1 CompilerThread0), the VM Thread, which runs operations that need every Java thread paused, and the Signal Dispatcher, which turns kill -3 into a thread dump. The two called java are the launcher thread from lesson 1, whose TID is the PID, and main.

Many of these counts follow the number of CPUs the JVM sees. The lab box has 12, so the JVM made 12 carrier threads for virtual threads, which the last section explains. Start the same program with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2 and it has 25 tasks.

So a JVM is never one thread. Before your code starts a single one, it is already a few dozen tasks, and every one of them is something the kernel schedules, counts and can show you.

try.title: Count a JVM's threads from outside
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. The demo is os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/PaymentWorkers.java: two sleeping ledger writers, one busy fraud scorer and 1,000 virtual threads.
Run the first block. Before the uniq line, guess which name will be the most common.
Then run the second block, which starts the same program as if the machine had 2 CPUs. Predict whether the task count goes up or down.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/*.java java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers 120 & pid=$! sleep 3 ls /proc/$pid/task | wc -l cat /proc/$pid/task/*/comm | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5 grep Threads /proc/$pid/status kill $pid java -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=2 -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers 120 & pid=$! sleep 3; ls /proc/$pid/task | wc -l; kill $pid

try.expect:
pid 41 running
36
     13 ForkJoinPool-1-
      2 java
      2 C2 CompilerThre
      1 VM Thread
      1 VM Periodic Tas
Threads:	36
pid 89 running
25

36 tasks, and 13 of them are the virtual-thread scheduler's pool: 12 carriers plus ForkJoinPool-1-delayScheduler, the pool's timer thread, which wakes the sleeping virtual threads. With ActiveProcessorCount=2 the pool shrinks to 2 carriers and the total drops to 25. Your counts depend on how many CPUs your Docker VM has (nproc tells you), and the JIT sometimes adds a second C2 compiler thread.

sections.h: A platform thread is one OS thread, and jstack knows which
sections.html:
When a service burns CPU, the two halves of the story live in different places. The kernel knows which task is using the CPU, by TID. The JVM knows what that thread is: its Java name and its stack trace, the chain of method calls it is in. To fix a hot loop you need both, joined on something they share.

The join is easy for the threads you usually create. Thread.ofPlatform().start(...), or the old new Thread(...).start(), ends in pthread_create, the C library's function for starting a thread, which ends in the clone you saw in the first section. From then on the Java thread and the task are one thing. The kernel schedules it, top shows its CPU use, and when it blocks in Thread.sleep or a socket read, the kernel puts that task to sleep. The JDK calls these platform threads.

Each platform thread also gets its own stack, and the JVM reserves the whole stack when it creates the thread. In the lab box that's about 2 MB per thread (when creation fails, the JVM's log line says stacksize: 2040k). On x86-64 Linux the default is 1 MB. Reserved isn't the same as used. The kernel sets the address range aside at once, but hands out real memory one 4 KB page at a time, as the thread first touches it.

jstack <pid> prints the JVM's side, and every thread's header line carries the TID. Here is the hot thread of the demo service, found from both sides:

$ ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3
  145 99.7 fraud-scorer
  123  0.3 java
  140  0.2 C1 CompilerThre
$ jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=145 "
"fraud-scorer" #27 [145] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=5142.71ms elapsed=5.14s tid=0x0000ffffa014db90 nid=145 runnable  [0x0000ffff753aa000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers.score(PaymentWorkers.java:45)

Read the header from left to right. fraud-scorer is the Java name. #27 is the Java thread ID, the number Thread.threadId() returns. [145] is the TID. cpu= is the CPU time this thread has used. tid=0x... is the address of the JVM's internal thread object, not an OS ID, despite its name. nid=145, the native ID, is the TID again.

On JDK 18 and later nid is decimal, so it matches top and ps as is. JDK 17 and older print it in hex, nid=0x91, and you convert first with printf '%x\n' 145. Plenty of runbooks still say to convert. On JDK 21 or 25 that sends you looking for a thread that isn't there.

That's the whole method for a hot thread in production: top -H -p <pid> or ps -L gives the TID, and the thread dump gives the Java stack for that TID. The lab builds the join as a small tool.

try.title: From a hot TID to a Java stack
steps: In the box, start the demo again and give the fraud scorer a few seconds to burn CPU.
List the threads by CPU use, take the top TID, and grep the thread dump for it. The HOT= line does the copy and paste for you.
Print the TID in hex too. That's what you'd search for on JDK 17.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers 120 & pid=$! sleep 5 ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3 HOT=$(ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu --no-headers | sort -k2 -nr | head -1 | awk '{print $1}') jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=$HOT " printf '%x\n' $HOT kill $pid

try.expect:
TIDs change on every run:

pid 121 running
  145 99.7 fraud-scorer
  123  0.3 java
  140  0.2 C1 CompilerThre
"fraud-scorer" #27 [145] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=5142.71ms elapsed=5.14s tid=0x0000ffffa014db90 nid=145 runnable  [0x0000ffff753aa000]
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers.score(PaymentWorkers.java:45)
	at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers$$Lambda/0x000007fe01040438.run(Unknown Source)
91

One thread uses a whole CPU, and the dump names the method: PaymentWorkers.score, line 45. cpu=5142.71ms after elapsed=5.14s says the same thing from the JVM's side. On JDK 17 the header would say nid=0x91.

sections.h: Every platform thread counts against the pids limit
sections.html:
A program that calls fork in a loop, where every child does the same, is called a fork bomb. It fills the kernel's table of tasks in seconds, and then nothing new can start, not even the shell you would use to stop it. On a host shared by many containers, one bad container would do that to all of them. So the kernel can cap the number of tasks per group of processes.

The groups are cgroups (control groups): sets of processes the kernel limits as one unit. Every container is one, and lesson 12 of this track takes them apart. The pids controller is the part of cgroups that caps tasks. Docker sets it with --pids-limit, and Kubernetes with the kubelet's podPidsLimit. Inside the container the limit is in /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max. A thread is a task, so every platform thread counts, along with every thread the JVM starts for itself and every process.

When the group is full, clone fails with EAGAIN ("try again later") and the JVM throws an error with a misleading name. Here is ThreadFlood, which starts platform threads that each wait (like requests waiting on a slow card issuer), in a container started with --pids-limit 64:

[0.322s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start thread "Unknown thread" - pthread_create failed (EAGAIN) for attributes: stacksize: 2040k, guardsize: 4k, detached.
[0.322s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start the native thread for java.lang.Thread "Thread-42"
failed after 42 platform threads: unable to create native thread: possibly out of memory or process/resource limits reached
OS threads in this JVM: 63

It got 42 threads. The JVM's own threads used most of the other 22 slots, and the container's shell used one. The error is an OutOfMemoryError, but the heap was nearly empty: the kernel refused a new task. In the same run the garbage collector also failed to start a worker (GC Thread#2), so a full pids limit hurts the JVM's own work too. The exact number changes from run to run (I've seen 42 and 50), because the JVM starts helper threads when it needs them.

So when you see "unable to create native thread", suspect a task limit before memory. The usual ones are the cgroup's pids.max and the per-user process limit (ulimit -u), which counts threads too. Inside a container, read /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.events first: its max counter goes up every time a fork or clone hits the limit.

try.title: Hit the pids limit with platform threads
steps: This one runs from the labs folder on your Mac, not inside the box: it starts a fresh container with a limit of 64 tasks.
Predict how many of the 200 platform threads start.
Run it and read the three parts of the output: the limit, the JVM's complaint, and the pids.events counter.

code.title: on your Mac, in labs/
code.html: docker run --rm --pids-limit 64 -v "$PWD":/labs -w /labs sfz-labbox:1 \ bash -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max; java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/ThreadFlood.java platform 200; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.events'

try.expect:
One run (yours will stop at a slightly different count):

64
[0.300s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start thread "GC Thread#2" - pthread_create failed (EAGAIN) for attributes: stacksize: 2040k, guardsize: 4k, detached.
[0.300s][error  ][gc,task  ] GC(0) Failed to create worker thread
...
[0.322s][warning][os,thread] Failed to start the native thread for java.lang.Thread "Thread-42"
failed after 42 platform threads: unable to create native thread: possibly out of memory or process/resource limits reached
OS threads in this JVM: 63
max 12

pthread_create failed (EAGAIN) is the kernel refusing a new task. The JVM turns it into an OutOfMemoryError with a heap that is almost empty. max 12 in pids.events says the group hit its limit 12 times, including the GC's failed attempts. The container is removed when the command ends.

sections.h: Virtual threads share a few carrier threads
sections.html:
Now scale the waiting up: 10,000 requests in flight, each waiting 120 ms on the issuer. As platform threads that's 10,000 tasks, about 20 GB of stack address space reserved, 10,000 entries against the pids limit, and a kernel juggling 10,000 sleepers. Most of that pays for waiting, not work.

One way out is asynchronous code. A few threads start each I/O and hand the rest of the work to a callback (CompletableFuture.thenCompose, reactive streams), so no thread sits blocked. It works, but the code turns into chains of callbacks, and a stack trace no longer shows how you got somewhere.

Virtual threads, final since JDK 21 (JEP 444), keep plain blocking code and move the switching from the kernel into the JDK. Run the same 10,000 waits on them in the same container, and nothing fails:

started 10,000 virtual threads
OS threads in this JVM: 37

A virtual thread is a Java object, not a task. To run, it mounts on a carrier: an ordinary platform thread from a ForkJoinPool that the JDK keeps for this job. By default there is one carrier per CPU, which is why the demo had 12 ForkJoinPool-1-worker threads in a box with 12 CPUs.

The trick happens when a virtual thread blocks. In Thread.sleep, a socket read, ReentrantLock.lock() or BlockingQueue.take(), the JDK unmounts it: it saves the thread's stack frames (one frame per method call in progress) on the heap and frees the carrier, which picks up another virtual thread. When the sleep ends or the data arrives, the virtual thread is queued again and mounts on whichever carrier is free. The kernel sees 12 busy tasks. Your code sees 10,000 threads that each block in plain, top-to-bottom style.

Some blocking still holds on to the carrier. This is called pinning. Up to JDK 23, blocking inside a synchronized block pinned, and JEP 491 removed that in JDK 24. Three cases still pin in JDK 25: blocking inside a class initializer (a static {} block), waiting for another thread to finish initializing a class, and blocking in native code that called back into Java. A pinned carrier can't run any other virtual thread, so 12 pinned virtual threads can stall every other virtual thread in a 12-carrier JVM.

Virtual threads don't make code faster. JEP 444 says so in as many words: "Virtual threads are not faster threads." They let far more tasks wait at once without a kernel task each. That suits a service that spends its time waiting on Oracle, Kafka or a card issuer, and does nothing for the CPU-bound fraud-scorer. Don't pool them either. Create one per task, and use a Semaphore to cap how many hit a downstream service at once.

jstack lists platform threads only, carriers included. The 1,000 virtual threads of the demo service aren't in it. To see virtual threads, use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file>.

stepper.title: A platform thread, then virtual threads on carriers
stepper.intro: Two carriers, three virtual threads and one platform thread. The TIDs come from the demo service in the lab box.

frames.say: V1 blocks inside a class's static {} initializer. That still pins in JDK 25: the JDK can't unmount V1, so worker-1 is stuck with it. Blocking inside synchronized pinned the same way until JEP 491 fixed it in JDK 24. If every carrier gets pinned, no other virtual thread in the JVM can run.

try.title: Run 10,000 virtual threads under the same limit
steps: Same container settings, same program, but virtual threads and 50 times as many of them. Predict the number of OS threads.
Run it from the labs folder on your Mac.

code.title: on your Mac, in labs/
code.html: docker run --rm --pids-limit 64 -v "$PWD":/labs -w /labs sfz-labbox:1 \ java os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l03/demo/ThreadFlood.java virtual 10000

try.expect:
started 10,000 virtual threads
OS threads in this JVM: 37

All 10,000 started and waited at once on about 37 OS threads: the JVM's usual helpers plus one carrier per CPU. The count changes a little between runs (I've seen 26 and 37) depending on which JIT and GC threads exist at that moment. Every virtual thread waits on a CountDownLatch, which unmounts it, so the carriers stay free.

refs.title: JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning

video.title: Context switches, blocking and virtual threads

analogy: Platform threads are like giving every payment request its own phone line to the card issuer. While a request waits on hold, its line is busy, and the exchange (the kernel) has a fixed number of lines per building (the pids limit). Virtual threads are a call centre: a few agents (carriers) work through thousands of open cases (virtual threads). When a case is waiting on the issuer, the agent files it (unmounts) and picks up the next one. When the issuer calls back, any free agent reopens the file. The analogy breaks on what the case file holds. An agent's case file is a few notes. A virtual thread's file is its whole call stack, copied to the heap and back, and some kinds of waiting (a class initializer, a native call) force the agent to stay on the line.
world: A Quarkus service with a 200-thread worker pool, a Kafka consumer pool and a JDBC pool can easily run 300 platform threads, plus the JVM's own. In a pod with a small podPidsLimit, a traffic spike that makes the pool grow ends in "unable to create native thread" with a healthy heap, and the dashboards point at memory. Check /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.events before you raise -Xmx. When one pod sits at 100% of a CPU, ps -L (or top -H) plus jstack names the thread and the method in under a minute, and on JDK 21 you grep for the decimal TID. Virtual threads fit the parts of a payment service that mostly wait: calls to the card issuer, Oracle queries, Temporal activity calls. Keep a Semaphore in front of each downstream service, because 10,000 virtual threads will happily open 10,000 requests to a service that can take 50.
mistake: Reading tid= in a thread dump as the OS thread ID. It sits right there in the header, it says "tid", and people paste it into top -H. It is the address of the JVM's internal thread structure, 0x0000ffffa014db90, and matches nothing in the kernel. The OS thread ID is nid (and, in JDK 25, the number in brackets after the Java ID). The second half of the same mistake is converting nid to hex on a modern JDK because an old runbook says so. Since JDK 18 nid is decimal and matches ps -L and top -H directly. Check which JDK the service runs before you convert anything.

compare.note: Same container, same JDK, same waiting code. Each platform thread is a kernel task with a 2 MB stack reserved, so the 64-task limit stops the program at 42 of its own threads. A virtual thread is a heap object that only needs a carrier while it runs, and a thread waiting on a latch unmounts, so 10,000 of them fit on the JVM's usual 37 or so OS threads. The limit didn't change. The number of tasks the program asked the kernel for did.

worked.title: Find the thread that's burning a CPU

steps.say: A ledger service's pod sits at 100% of one CPU and latency is up. First, find which thread uses the CPU, from the kernel's side. ps -L lists threads with their CPU share. In the demo, one TID stands out.
steps.code: ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3 # 145 99.7 fraud-scorer # 123 0.3 java # 140 0.2 C1 CompilerThre

steps.say: Then ask the JVM what that thread is doing. On JDK 18 and later, search the dump for the TID as it is. jcmd <pid> Thread.print prints the same dump if jstack isn't installed.
steps.code: jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=145 " # "fraud-scorer" #27 [145] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=5142.71ms elapsed=5.14s ... nid=145 runnable # java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE # at sfz.os.l03.demo.PaymentWorkers.score(PaymentWorkers.java:45)

steps.say: On JDK 17 or older, the dump shows nid in hex. Convert the TID first, then search.
steps.code: printf '%x\n' 145 # 91 jstack $pid | grep -A3 "nid=0x91 "

steps.say: Take two or three dumps a few seconds apart. If the same frame is on top every time, that method is the loop to look at. If the hot TID belongs to a thread with no # number, such as GC Thread#0 or C2 CompilerThread0, the CPU goes to the JVM itself: heavy garbage collection points to allocation, and a busy compiler usually settles after warm-up. If the hot TID is not in the dump at all, check whether it is the launcher thread (TID = PID) or a thread that native code started.

lab.title: Join the kernel's threads to the JVM's
steps: Open the two captured files. They are real output from this lesson's demo in the lab box: ps -L -p <pid> -o tid,pcpu,time,comm, and jstack <pid> a moment later.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All eight fail.
Write ThreadDump.nidToTid: hex when the text starts with 0x, decimal otherwise.

Write ThreadDump.parse. Match each line against HEADER. For each header, the thread's own lines run until the next blank line. Take the state from the line that starts with java.lang.Thread.State: (first word only) and the top frame from the first line that starts with at (trim first).
Write the three ThreadMap methods. Build a Map<Int, DumpedThread> keyed by osTid once and use it in all three.
Run the tests until all eight pass. Then look at what tasksNotInDump returns and say which thread that is.
hints: HEADER.find(line) returns null for every line that isn't a thread header, including the dump's date and title lines.
lines.drop(i + 1).takeWhile { it.isNotBlank() } gives the lines that belong to the header at index i.
The dump also has a thread the ps file doesn't: Attach Listener. jstack itself made the JVM start it, after ps had already run.

drill.title: Hot TID to Java stack, from memory
drill.prompt: Write the commands that take you from "this JVM uses a whole CPU" to the Java stack of the thread responsible, on JDK 25. Then write what changes on JDK 17. Check against the answer.

answer.html: pid=$(pgrep -f ledger-service) # or: jcmd -l ps -L -p $pid -o tid,pcpu,comm | sort -k2 -nr | head -3 # or: top -H -p $pid jstack $pid | grep -A10 "nid=145 " # JDK 18+: nid is decimal # JDK 17 and older: nid is hex printf '%x\n' 145 # 91 jstack $pid | grep -A10 "nid=0x91 "

recap: Linux schedules tasks. A thread is a task made by clone with flags that share memory, files and signal handlers. A process is a group of tasks, and its PID is the first task's TID.
Each thread has a directory under /proc/<pid>/task/. The kernel keeps only 15 characters of a thread name, so join on TIDs, never names.
A platform thread is one OS thread for life, with about 2 MB of stack reserved on arm64 Linux (1 MB on x86-64). jstack shows its TID as [145] and nid=145; JDK 17 and older print nid in hex.
The pids limit counts threads. When it's reached, clone fails with EAGAIN and the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread.
Virtual threads mount on a few carriers, one per CPU by default, and unmount when they block. Since JDK 24 synchronized doesn't pin; class initializers and native frames still do.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to move a Kafka consumer service from a 200-thread pool to virtual threads "to make it faster". Explain what virtual threads change at the OS level, and when the move helps.
explain.answer: Today each of the 200 pool threads is an OS thread: the kernel schedules it, it has a couple of megabytes of stack reserved, and it counts against the pod's pids limit. While a thread waits on Oracle or an HTTP call, its OS thread sleeps and does nothing else. Virtual threads are Java objects. They run by mounting on a handful of carrier threads, about one per CPU, and when they block on I/O the JDK saves their frames on the heap and frees the carrier. So we could have thousands of handlers waiting at once on a dozen OS threads. That helps if the handlers mostly wait and the pool size is what limits throughput. It does nothing for CPU-bound work, and each handler isn't any faster. We'd also keep a limit on concurrency with a semaphore, so we don't flood Oracle, and check that no handler blocks inside a class initializer or a native call, which would pin a carrier.

deeper.html:
jstack can't show virtual threads, but jcmd can write a JSON dump that groups every thread by the container that owns it. For the demo service in the lab box (summarized with a few lines of Python):

$ jcmd $pid Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/threads.json
<root>                                                    11 threads
ForkJoinPool-1/jdk.internal.vm.SharedThreadContainer@...  13 threads
java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@133c6e62     1000 threads

The 1,000 are the virtual threads from newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), each with "virtual": true, an empty name and a stack that ends in Thread.sleep. Their tid values are Java thread IDs. A virtual thread has no OS thread ID of its own, because it has no OS thread.

The carrier pool's size comes from jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, which defaults to the number of CPUs the JVM sees. That means -XX:ActiveProcessorCount and a container's CPU limit both change it, as the Try-it showed.

Thread stacks are another reason platform threads cost more than they look. The JVM reserves the whole stack when it creates the thread, about 2 MB on arm64 Linux, plus a guard page that crashes the thread cleanly on overflow instead of letting it write into its neighbour's memory. That reservation shows up in the process's virtual size (VSZ) right away. Resident memory (RSS) grows only as the thread actually uses its stack, page by page. Lesson 6 of this track explains how the kernel does that. Until then, remember that 500 threads reserve about 1 GB of address space and might use only a few dozen megabytes of real memory.

JDK 25's thread list also has two names you won't find in a JDK 21 dump. VirtualThread-unblocker came with JEP 491 in JDK 24: it asks the VM for virtual threads that may continue after waiting on a synchronized monitor and gives them back to the scheduler. ForkJoinPool-1-delayScheduler is the carrier pool's timer thread. The pool starts it the first time something schedules a delayed task, and in the demo that something was 1,000 sleeping virtual threads waiting for their wake-up time.
